title: Percentiles, quartiles and the interquartile range
summary: What a percentile means, the index rule for computing it, quartiles as special percentiles, the quartile formulas for raw and grouped data, and the IQR.

chunks.heading: What a percentile tells you
chunks.explanation_md:
Mean, median and mode describe the centre. A **percentile** does something else: it **provides information about how the data are spread over the interval from the smallest value to the largest value**.

The definition to learn word for word:

> The **pth percentile** of a data set is a value such that **at least p per cent** of the items take on **this value or less**, and **at least (100 - p) per cent** of the items take on **this value or more**.

So every percentile splits the data into two sides: p per cent at or below it, (100 - p) per cent at or above it.

key_terms.meaning: A value such that at least p per cent of the items take on this value or less, and at least (100 - p) per cent take on this value or more.

chunks.exam_line: The pth percentile: at least p per cent of items take this value or less, and at least (100 - p) per cent take this value or more.

chunks.heading: Computing a percentile: the index rule
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide gives three steps.

**Step 1:** arrange the data in **ascending order**.

**Step 2:** compute the index **i**, the **position** of the pth percentile:

i = (p/100) × n

**Step 3:** read off the value, and here the rule splits:

- **If i is not an integer, round up.** The pth percentile is the value in the **ith position**.
- **If i is an integer**, the pth percentile is the **average of the values in the ith and (i + 1)th positions**.

**Quick try:** the 50th percentile of the 8 sorted values from the median example (12, 14, 18, 19, 26, 27, 27, 30).

i = (50/100) × 8 = 4. That is an integer, so average the 4th and 5th values: (19 + 26)/2 = **22.5**.

That is exactly the median the slide found for those values, which fits the next slide: the 50th percentile is the median.
chunks.exam_line: i = (p/100) × n. Not an integer: round up and take the ith value. An integer: average the ith and (i + 1)th values.

chunks.heading: Quartiles are specific percentiles
chunks.explanation_md:
**Quartiles are specific percentiles.** For better analysis, the data distribution can be subdivided into **four groups**, known as **quartiles**:

- **First Quartile (Q1) = 25th Percentile**
- **Second Quartile (Q2) = 50th Percentile = Median**
- **Third Quartile (Q3) = 75th Percentile**

The quartile picture lays them on a line from **Min** to **Max**: Q1, then the **Median (Q2)**, then Q3.

- From Min to Q1 covers **25%** of the data.
- From Min to the Median covers **50%**, and from the Median to Max the other **50%**.
- From Min to Q3 covers **75%**.

key_terms.meaning: The 50th percentile, which is the median.

chunks.exam_line: Q1 = 25th percentile, Q2 = 50th percentile = median, Q3 = 75th percentile.

chunks.heading: Quartile formulas for ungrouped (raw) data
chunks.explanation_md:
For **ungrouped (raw) data**, sorted in ascending order, the slide gives positions:

- **Q1 = ((n + 1)/4)th term**
- **Q2 = ((n + 1)/2)th term (Median)**
- **Q3 = (3(n + 1)/4)th term**

Notice Q2 is the same position formula as the median for an odd number of observations.

**Try it** on the median example's 7 sorted values: 12, 14, 18, 19, 26, 27, 27 (n = 7, so n + 1 = 8).

- Q1: 8/4 = 2nd term = **14**
- Q2: 8/2 = 4th term = **19** (the median the slide found)
- Q3: 3 × 8/4 = 6th term = **27**
chunks.exam_line: Raw data: Q1 = ((n + 1)/4)th term, Q2 = ((n + 1)/2)th term (median), Q3 = (3(n + 1)/4)th term.

chunks.heading: Grouped data, and the interquartile range (IQR)
chunks.explanation_md:
For **grouped data (class intervals)** the slide gives one formula for any quartile:

Qk = L + ((k · n/4 - F) / f) · h

where:

- **Qk**: the k-th quartile (k = 1, 2, 3)
- **L**: lower boundary of the quartile class
- **n**: total frequency
- **F**: cumulative frequency before the quartile class
- **f**: frequency of the quartile class
- **h**: width of the class interval

**Interquartile Range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1**

**Purpose of IQR:**

- Measures the **spread of the middle 50%** of the data.
- Useful for identifying **outliers** and understanding **data variability**.
- **Less affected by extreme values than the range.**

For the 7 values in the previous chunk: IQR = 27 - 14 = **13**.

key_terms.meaning: Q3 - Q1: the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

chunks.exam_line: Grouped: Qk = L + ((k · n/4 - F)/f) · h. IQR = Q3 - Q1, the spread of the middle 50%, less affected by extreme values than the range.

questions.stem: Using the 20 net worths sorted on the practice slide, find Q1 and Q3 with the percentile index rule, and calculate the interquartile range.
questions.model_answer_md:
Quartiles are specific percentiles: **Q1 = 25th percentile**, **Q3 = 75th percentile**.

**Sorted data (n = 20):** 18, 18, 18, 18, **19, 20**, 20, 20, 21, 22, 22, 23, 24, 26, **27, 32**, 33, 49, 52, 56

**Index rule:** i = (p/100) x n; if i is an integer, average the ith and (i + 1)th values.

- **Q1:** i = (25/100) x 20 = 5, an integer. Average the 5th and 6th values: (19 + 20)/2 = **19.5**
- **Q3:** i = (75/100) x 20 = 15, an integer. Average the 15th and 16th values: (27 + 32)/2 = **29.5**
- **IQR = Q3 - Q1** = 29.5 - 19.5 = **10**

The middle 50% of these net worths lie within a band of $10 billion, even though the full data run up to 56: the IQR is less affected by extreme values.

rubric.point: Q1 = 25th and Q3 = 75th percentile
IQR = 29.5 - 19.5 = 10; less affected by extreme values

questions.stem: Using the raw-data quartile formulas, find Q1, Q2 and Q3 of the 15 retail stores' monthly sales and calculate the IQR.
questions.model_answer_md:
For ungrouped data, the slide gives the **position** of each quartile.

**Sorted sales (₹ lakhs, n = 15):** 27, 28, 29, **30**, 30, 31, 32, **34**, 34, 35, 36, **38**, 39, 41, 44. So n + 1 = 16.

- **Q1 = ((n + 1)/4)th term** = (16/4) = 4th term = **30**
- **Q2 = ((n + 1)/2)th term** = (16/2) = 8th term = **34** (the median)
- **Q3 = (3(n + 1)/4)th term** = (3 x 16/4) = 12th term = **38**
- **IQR = Q3 - Q1** = 38 - 30 = **8**

The middle half of the stores sell between ₹30 and ₹38 lakhs a month.

rubric.point: Sort and use n + 1 = 16
Q1 = 4th term = 30
Q2 = 8th term = 34 (median)
Q3 = 12th term = 38; IQR = 8

questions.stem: Differentiate between a percentile and a quartile.
questions.model_answer_md:
Both describe how data are spread from the smallest to the largest value.

| Basis | Percentile | Quartile |
|---|---|---|
| **Meaning** | The **pth percentile** has at least p% of items at or below it and at least (100 - p)% at or above it | **Specific percentiles** that split the data into **four groups** |
| **How many** | Any p from the range | Three: Q1, Q2, Q3 |
| **Link** | 25th, 50th, 75th | Q1 = 25th, **Q2 = 50th = median**, Q3 = 75th |

Every quartile is a percentile, but not every percentile is a quartile.

rubric.point: Percentile definition: at least p% at or below, at least (100 - p)% at or above
Quartiles are specific percentiles dividing data into four groups
Q1 = 25th, Q2 = 50th = median, Q3 = 75th

questions.stem: Define the pth percentile and explain the slide's three-step method for computing it. Illustrate both cases of the rule: the 80th percentile of the 70 values (i = 56) and the 90th percentile of the 15 retail stores' sales.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **percentile** tells how the data are **spread over the interval from the smallest to the largest value**.

**Definition:** the **pth percentile** is a value such that **at least p per cent** of the items take on this value **or less**, and **at least (100 - p) per cent** take on this value **or more**.

**Three-step method:**
1. **Arrange the data in ascending order.**
2. **Compute the index** i = (p/100) x n, the position of the pth percentile.
3. **Read off the value:**
   - if **i is not an integer, round up**: the percentile is the value in the ith position;
   - if **i is an integer**, the percentile is the **average of the values in the ith and (i + 1)th positions**.

**Case 1: i is an integer (70 values).**
- i = (80/100) x 70 = **56**.
- Average the 56th and 57th values: (535 + 549)/2 = **542**.
- Check with the definition: 56/70 = .8, so at least **80%** are 542 or less; 14/70 = .2, so at least **20%** are 542 or more.

**Case 2: i is not an integer (15 stores).**
- Sorted sales: 27, 28, 29, 30, 30, 31, 32, 34, 34, 35, 36, 38, 39, **41**, 44.
- i = (90/100) x 15 = 13.5, not an integer, so **round up to 14**.
- The 14th value is **41**: the 90th percentile is ₹41 lakhs, and stores 4 (41) and 12 (44) form the top 10%.

**Conclusion:** sort, compute i, then either average two neighbouring values (integer i) or round up and take one value (non-integer i).

rubric.point: Percentile: spread from smallest to largest; pth percentile definition
Step 1 sort; step 2 i = (p/100)n
Integer i: average ith and (i + 1)th; non-integer: round up
15 stores: i = 13.5, round up to 14th value = 41
